commands.name: C program structure
commands.summary: Headers, declarations, functions, and the program entry point.
commands.description: A hosted C program normally enters through main. Headers declare library interfaces; declarations make types and functions known. Each statement usually ends with a semicolon. A successful main can return 0.

examples.description: A complete C99 program using a standard library function.

commands.note: C programs are compiled; Bash scripts are interpreted by a shell.

commands.name: Comments (// and /* */)
commands.summary: Annotate source without executing the text.
commands.description: C99 supports // line comments and /* ... */ block comments. Block comments cannot be nested. Comment intent, assumptions, and non-obvious behavior rather than restating every statement.

examples.description: Both comment forms are ignored by the compiler.

commands.name: #include
commands.summary: Include declarations from a header.
commands.description: The preprocessor replaces an include directive with a header's contents. Angle brackets select an implementation's header search; quotes usually search locally first. Prefer standard headers for standard library declarations.

examples.description: The standard header makes puts available.

commands.note: Include guards or #pragma once can prevent repeated custom-header definitions.

commands.name: #define
commands.summary: Define a macro or symbolic constant.
commands.description: Object-like macros substitute tokens before compilation; function-like macros also substitute arguments. Macro arguments can be evaluated more than once, so use functions for operations with side effects. Parenthesize macro parameters.

examples.description: Defines a constant-like macro and a guarded expression macro.

commands.note: Avoid SQUARE(i++) because the argument is used twice.

commands.name: #if / #ifdef / #ifndef
commands.summary: Compile selected source based on macros.
commands.description: Conditional preprocessing evaluates constant integer preprocessor expressions. #ifdef tests whether a macro exists, while #ifndef tests its absence. This is often used for conditional builds and header guards.

examples.description: Only one branch survives preprocessing.

commands.name: #undef
commands.summary: Remove an existing macro definition.
commands.description: #undef makes a macro name undefined for subsequent preprocessing. It does not change C variables or runtime storage.

examples.description: The conditional sees MODE as undefined.

commands.name: Identifiers and scope
commands.summary: Names obey declaration, scope, and linkage rules.
commands.description: Local variables declared inside a block have block scope. File-scope declarations are visible from their declaration to the end of the translation unit. Scope is not the same as lifetime or linkage.

examples.description: An inner block can hide an outer declaration.

commands.name: C language versions
commands.summary: C99, C11, C17, and C23 are different standards.
commands.description: C99 introduced mixed declarations and statements, // comments, and other facilities. C11 added features such as _Static_assert and _Generic. C17 largely fixes C11 defects. C23 adds further language and library changes; support varies by compiler.

examples.description: An explicitly selected standard avoids depending on the compiler default.

commands.note: This reference mainly targets ISO C99 unless an entry says otherwise.

commands.name: const
commands.summary: Prevent modification through a declared object or access path.
commands.description: A const-qualified object cannot be modified through an lvalue of const-qualified type. For pointers, const can apply to the pointed-to object, the pointer itself, or both. const does not imply a compile-time integer constant in C.

examples.description: The value can be read through a pointer to const.

commands.note: Casting away const and modifying an object originally declared const is undefined behavior.

commands.name: volatile
commands.summary: Tell the compiler an object's value may change unexpectedly.
commands.description: volatile-qualified accesses are observable for the abstract machine and are useful for some memory-mapped I/O situations. volatile does not make access atomic or synchronize threads.

examples.description: Shows syntax; volatile is typically motivated by hardware or signal contexts.

commands.note: Use atomics for inter-thread synchronization; volatile is not a substitute.

commands.name: typedef
commands.summary: Give an existing type an alias.
commands.description: A typedef creates a type name, not a new distinct type. It can simplify complex pointer or function pointer declarations, but avoid hiding important pointer semantics.

examples.description: Defines and uses a convenient alias.

commands.name: sizeof
commands.summary: Get the size of a type or object in bytes.
commands.description: sizeof evaluates to a value of type size_t. Except for variable-length array operands, its operand expression is not evaluated. For arrays in their declared scope, sizeof yields the whole array's byte size; after array-to-pointer conversion it yields pointer size.

examples.description: Calculates element count while numbers is an array.

commands.note: sizeof(char) is exactly 1; the number of bits per byte is CHAR_BIT.

commands.name: _Static_assert
commands.summary: Check a constant condition at compile time (C11).
commands.description: _Static_assert requires a constant expression and a diagnostic string in C11/C17. It is useful for validating representation assumptions during compilation.

examples.description: A C11 compile-time check; compile with -std=c11.

commands.note: For a C99-only course, use another technique or omit this feature.

commands.name: int
commands.summary: Store an integer within an implementation-defined range.
commands.description: int is a signed integer type. Its minimum required range is at least -32767 through 32767, although many platforms provide 32-bit int. Use limits.h for actual ranges; do not assume all int values are 32 bits.

examples.description: Declares and prints an int using %d.

commands.name: unsigned int
commands.summary: Store nonnegative integers with modulo arithmetic.
commands.description: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N, where N is the number of value bits. Mixing signed and unsigned types may produce unexpected comparisons or conversions.

examples.description: Prints an unsigned int with %u.

commands.note: Do not rely on unsigned wraparound to detect signed overflow.

commands.name: char
commands.summary: Store one byte of character or numeric data.
commands.description: char, signed char, and unsigned char are three distinct types. Plain char may be signed or unsigned depending on the implementation. Character literals such as 'A' have type int in C.

examples.description: Prints a character and its numeric value.

commands.note: Portable code should not assume the execution character set is ASCII.

commands.name: short / long / long long
commands.summary: Choose integer ranks and minimum guaranteed ranges.
commands.description: short is at least 16 bits, long at least 32 bits, and long long at least 64 bits. Exact widths are implementation-defined. Add U or L/LL suffixes to literals when appropriate.

examples.description: Uses the C99 long long type and matching format specifier.

commands.name: float / double / long double
commands.summary: Represent floating-point values with differing precision/range.
commands.description: Floating-point arithmetic is typically approximate; decimal fractions often cannot be stored exactly. Use %f for double with printf (float promotes), and %Lf for long double. scanf requires %f for float and %lf for double.

examples.description: Formats a floating-point value to two decimal places.

commands.note: Avoid comparing computed floating-point results for exact equality when rounding matters.

commands.name: _Bool / bool
commands.summary: Represent logical truth as 0 or 1.
commands.description: C99 defines _Bool. Include stdbool.h to use bool, true, and false macros in C99/C17. Conversion to _Bool stores 0 for zero and 1 for any nonzero scalar.

examples.description: Uses C99 stdbool.h for readable Boolean declarations.

commands.note: C and C++ differ in Boolean keyword details; do not assume they are identical.

commands.name: size_t
commands.summary: Represent sizes and counts returned by sizeof.
commands.description: size_t is an unsigned integer type defined by several standard headers, including stddef.h and stdio.h. Use %zu for printf in C99. Subtracting from zero wraps, so be careful with reverse loops.
commands.syntax: size_t count = sizeof array / sizeof array[0];

examples.description: Prints an object count portably.

commands.name: ptrdiff_t
commands.summary: Store differences between pointers into the same array.
commands.description: ptrdiff_t is a signed integer type defined in stddef.h. Subtracting pointers to elements of the same array (or one-past) yields an element difference, provided it is representable.

examples.description: Shows subtraction of pointers within a single array.

commands.name: stdint.h fixed-width types
commands.summary: Request integer types with explicit widths when available.
commands.description: stdint.h defines types such as int32_t and uint64_t if those exact-width types are supported, plus guaranteed minimum-width types such as int_least32_t. inttypes.h provides PRI... macros for portable printf formats.

examples.description: Uses a minimum-width integer and its matching print macro.

commands.name: enum
commands.summary: Define named integer constants as an enumeration.
commands.description: An enum declares a set of integer constants. In C99 the compatible integer type of an enum is implementation-defined; an enumerator is an int constant when its value is representable. Use enum for states and choices.

examples.description: Defines a small, named set of integer values.

commands.name: struct
commands.summary: Group related members into one object.
commands.description: A structure's members are accessed with .; a pointer to a structure uses ->. Member layout may contain padding. Assignment copies a whole struct value, including array members.
commands.syntax: struct Point { int x; int y; };

examples.description: Defines, initializes, and accesses structure members.

commands.name: union
commands.summary: Allow several members to share storage.
commands.description: A union has overlapping members: its size is sufficient for its largest member, possibly plus padding. The interpretation of a stored member must follow the language's effective-type and union-access rules.
commands.syntax: union Number { int i; double d; };

examples.description: Writes and reads the same active union member.

commands.note: Do not assume reading a different member is a portable numeric conversion.

commands.name: storage duration: auto / static / extern
commands.summary: Distinguish lifetime, visibility, and cross-file linkage.
commands.description: Automatic local objects typically exist during block execution. Static storage-duration objects exist for the program lifetime and are initialized once. At file scope, static also gives internal linkage; extern commonly declares an object defined elsewhere.

examples.description: Shows a variable with static storage duration.

commands.note: static has different linkage effects at file scope versus function scope.

commands.name: integer literals
commands.summary: Write integer constants in decimal, octal, or hexadecimal.
commands.description: A leading 0 denotes octal in C99, while 0x denotes hexadecimal. Suffixes U, L, and LL affect candidate types. Integer literal types are chosen by value, base, suffix, and standard rules.

examples.description: Decimal 42 and hexadecimal 0x2A represent the same integer.

commands.name: character and string literals
commands.summary: Write characters, escape sequences, and null-terminated text.
commands.description: 'A' is a character constant (type int in C), whereas "A" is an array of two char elements including '\0'. Common escapes include '\n', '\t', '\\', and '\"'.

examples.description: Contrasts a character value with a string literal.

commands.note: Modifying a string literal has undefined behavior in C.

commands.name: initialization and = assignment
commands.summary: Set initial values or update existing objects.
commands.description: Initialization occurs when an object is created; assignment changes an already-existing modifiable object. An uninitialized automatic scalar usually has an indeterminate value and must not be read.

examples.description: Updates a previously initialized integer.

commands.name: explicit cast
commands.summary: Request a conversion to a chosen type.
commands.description: A C cast uses (type)expression. Casting integers to floating point before division changes the operation performed. A cast cannot make an invalid pointer conversion safe by itself.

examples.description: Converts one operand before division to avoid integer division.

commands.note: Casting away type incompatibilities does not remove undefined behavior.

commands.name: arithmetic + - * / %
commands.summary: Add, subtract, multiply, divide, or take remainder.
commands.description: Integer division truncates toward zero in C99 and later. % applies to integers and yields the remainder with sign related to the left operand. Signed overflow is undefined behavior; division by zero is undefined.
commands.syntax: a + b; a - b; a * b; a / b; a % b;

examples.description: Integer division gives quotient 2 and remainder 1.

commands.note: For negative operands, C remainder is not always mathematical modulo.

commands.name: comparison == != < <= > >=
commands.summary: Compare values to produce 0 or 1.
commands.description: == checks equality and = assigns; they are not interchangeable. Results of relational and equality operators have type int. For floating values, exact equality can be surprising due to rounding.
commands.syntax: a == b; a != b; a < b;

examples.description: Comparisons evaluate to 1 (true) or 0 (false).

commands.name: logical && || !
commands.summary: Combine truth values with short-circuit evaluation.
commands.description: && evaluates the right operand only if the left is true; || evaluates the right only if the left is false. ! reverses truth. Results are int 0 or 1. Short-circuiting is often used to check a pointer before dereferencing it.

examples.description: Demonstrates conjunction, disjunction, and negation.

commands.name: bitwise & | ^ ~
commands.summary: Operate on individual integer bits.
commands.description: &, |, ^, and ~ perform bitwise AND, OR, XOR, and complement. Unlike && and ||, bitwise binary operators do not short-circuit. Prefer unsigned operands for predictable bit manipulation.
commands.syntax: mask & flag; mask | flag; a ^ b; ~a;

examples.description: Bitwise operations on 6 (110) and 3 (011).

commands.name: shifts << >>
commands.summary: Shift integer bit patterns left or right.
commands.description: For unsigned left shift, the result is reduced modulo the unsigned type's range. The shift count must be nonnegative and smaller than the width of the promoted left operand. Right shift of negative signed values is implementation-defined in C99.

examples.description: Shifting 1U left by 3 produces 8.

commands.note: Left shifting a signed negative value is undefined behavior.

commands.name: increment ++ and decrement --
commands.summary: Increase or decrease a modifiable arithmetic value by one.
commands.description: Prefix ++i updates before producing the new value; postfix i++ produces the old value and updates the object. Both change the object; avoid unsequenced multiple modifications of the same variable.

examples.description: Postfix returns the previous value while incrementing i.

commands.note: Expressions like i = i++ + 1 have undefined behavior.

commands.name: compound assignments += -= *= /= %=
commands.summary: Update a value using an arithmetic operation.
commands.description: a += b is similar to a = a + b, except the left operand is evaluated only once. Other compound assignments include &=, |=, ^=, <<=, and >>=.

examples.description: Updates x without repeating its name.

commands.name: conditional ?:
commands.summary: Select one of two expressions based on a condition.
commands.description: The conditional operator evaluates only one of its second or third operands. It is an expression and can be used for short value selections; use if/else for more involved branches.

examples.description: Chooses the expression based on x > 5.

commands.name: comma operator
commands.summary: Evaluate two expressions in order and yield the second.
commands.description: The comma operator sequences its left operand before its right operand. It is different from commas separating function arguments or declarations, which are not the comma operator.

examples.description: The left expression executes before the right one.

commands.name: address-of & and dereference *
commands.summary: Compare address-of (&) with dereference (*) in expressions.
commands.description: After a declaration, unary &x produces a pointer to x (its address); unary *p accesses the object p points to. If x is int, &x has type int*; if p is int*, *p is an int lvalue that can be read or assigned. These operations work in opposite directions: object to pointer, and pointer to object. A pointer must point to a live suitable object before it is dereferenced. In a declaration such as int *p, * has a different grammatical role: it declares p as a pointer.
commands.syntax:
int x = 7;
int *p = &x;  // declaration *; expression &
int y = *p;   // expression * reads x
*p = 9;      // expression * writes x

examples.description: The declaration uses * to declare p; &x provides its address; *p accesses x afterwards.

options.description: Get the address of object x; result is a pointer (int* when x is int).
Access the object pointed to by p; read or modify it (int when p is int*).
In int *p, declare p as a pointer to int; no dereference occurs.

commands.note: In other contexts, binary * is multiplication and binary & is bitwise AND. Dereferencing NULL or an invalid pointer has undefined behavior.

commands.name: array subscript []
commands.summary: Access an element through a pointer plus index.
commands.description: a[i] is defined in terms of *(a + i). The index must identify a valid element for dereference. C does not check bounds automatically.

examples.description: Reads the second element, because indices start at zero.

commands.name: member access . and ->
commands.summary: Read a struct or union member directly or through a pointer.
commands.description: Use object.member for an object; use pointer->member for a pointer to a struct or union. p->x means (*p).x.

examples.description: Shows equivalent direct and pointer member access.

commands.name: operator precedence
commands.summary: Know how expressions group before evaluation.
commands.description: Precedence determines parsing; associativity breaks grouping ties. Neither determines the runtime evaluation order of all operands. Parentheses improve clarity for mixed logical and arithmetic expressions.

examples.description: Multiplication binds more tightly than addition.

commands.name: type conversions and promotions
commands.summary: Understand integer promotions and usual arithmetic conversions.
commands.description: Small integer types generally promote to int or unsigned int before many operations. Mixed signed/unsigned expressions follow conversion rules that can affect comparisons. Cast explicitly when a conversion is intentional.

examples.description: Illustrates integer division versus floating division.

commands.name: sequence and undefined behavior
commands.summary: Avoid unsequenced reads and writes to one scalar object.
commands.description: C evaluates some subexpressions in unspecified order. If two unsequenced side effects modify the same scalar, or a modification is unsequenced relative to a value computation of that object, behavior is undefined.

examples.description: Separate statements establish a clear order.

commands.note: Do not write printf("%d %d", i++, i++) or similar unsequenced modifications.

commands.name: if / else
commands.summary: Execute blocks depending on an expression's truth value.
commands.description: In C, zero is false and any nonzero scalar is true. Braces prevent accidental attachment of a later statement to the wrong branch.

examples.description: Selects one branch using an integer comparison.

commands.name: switch / case / default
commands.summary: Dispatch among integral constant labels.
commands.description: switch evaluates its controlling expression once and transfers to a matching case or default. Cases fall through unless execution exits, often via break. Case labels must be integer constant expressions.

examples.description: Shows explicit break statements to prevent fallthrough.

commands.name: for loop
commands.summary: Repeat initialization, condition check, and iteration expression.
commands.description: A for loop first runs initialization, then tests the condition before each iteration and executes the update afterward. In C99, loop-local declarations in for are supported.

examples.description: Prints indices 0 through 3.

commands.name: while loop
commands.summary: Repeat while a condition is true.
commands.description: A while loop checks its condition before each iteration, so the body may execute zero times. Update state or read new input so that a loop can terminate.

examples.description: Counts down until the condition becomes false.

commands.name: do / while loop
commands.summary: Execute a loop body at least once.
commands.description: A do/while loop checks the condition after the body. The trailing semicolon is required.

examples.description: The body executes before the false condition is checked.

commands.name: break / continue
commands.summary: Leave a loop or skip to its next iteration.
commands.description: break exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch. continue skips to the next iteration of the nearest enclosing loop; in a for loop the iteration expression runs before the next condition check.

examples.description: Skips 2 and exits before printing 5.

commands.name: return
commands.summary: Finish a function and optionally supply its result.
commands.description: return expression ends the current function and returns a value that is converted to the function's return type. In a void function use return; or reach the closing brace. main returning 0 conventionally signals success.

examples.description: Returns successful status from main.

commands.name: goto / labels
commands.summary: Jump to a labeled statement in the same function.
commands.description: goto can be used to centralize cleanup in C when several resources need release, but most ordinary control flow is clearer with loops and functions. It cannot jump between functions.

examples.description: Demonstrates a local jump target.

commands.name: function definition
commands.summary: Declare parameters, a return type, and a function body.
commands.description: A function definition includes executable statements. In C99, all called functions should have declarations in scope; implicit function declarations are not permitted.
commands.syntax: int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

examples.description: Defines a reusable function and calls it.

commands.name: function prototype
commands.summary: Declare a function's interface before defining it.
commands.description: A prototype tells the compiler the parameter types and result type, allowing calls before the definition. int f(void) declares no parameters; int f() in C99 is not a prototype and should usually be avoided.

examples.description: The definition appears after main because the prototype came first.

commands.name: pass by value
commands.summary: Function parameters are independent local objects.
commands.description: In C, arguments are passed by value. To update an object in the caller, pass a pointer to it. Passing a struct copies the struct; passing an array argument converts it to a pointer.

examples.description: The caller's integer remains unchanged.

commands.name: recursion
commands.summary: Let a function call itself with a smaller subproblem.
commands.description: Correct recursion needs a base case and progress toward it. Each call consumes stack resources, so deep recursion may exhaust available stack space. Iteration is often preferable for simple long-running traversals.
commands.syntax: int f(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * f(n - 1); }

examples.description: A small factorial example with a base case.

commands.note: The example assumes nonnegative small n; int factorial overflows for larger inputs.

commands.name: static local variable
commands.summary: Retain a local variable's value across function calls.
commands.description: A static local variable has block scope but static storage duration. It is initialized once (and zero-initialized when no initializer is supplied), not on each call.

examples.description: Two calls update one static local object; argument evaluation order is unspecified.

commands.note: The two printf arguments are evaluated in unspecified order; use separate statements when order matters.

commands.name: inline function
commands.summary: Suggest that a function definition is suitable for inline substitution.
commands.description: inline is a language linkage/inlining facility, not a promise that the compiler inserts code at the call site. C99 external-linkage rules differ from C++; static inline in a header is a common simple pattern.
commands.syntax: static inline int max2(int a, int b) { return a > b ? a : b; }

examples.description: Uses a small internal-linkage inline helper.

commands.note: Do not assume inline eliminates a call or changes observable semantics.

commands.name: function pointers
commands.summary: Store the address of a callable function.
commands.description: A function pointer's type includes parameter and return types. Parentheses around (*name) distinguish a pointer from a function returning a pointer.

examples.description: Calls a function through a pointer with a matching signature.

commands.name: variadic functions
commands.summary: Accept a variable number of arguments through stdarg.h.
commands.description: Use va_list, va_start, va_arg, and va_end to traverse unnamed arguments. The caller and callee must agree on count/types; default argument promotions apply.

examples.description: Adds three int arguments using C99 variable-argument facilities.

commands.note: Using va_arg with the wrong promoted type is undefined behavior.

commands.name: pointer declaration
commands.summary: Declare a variable that holds an address.
commands.description: In a declaration, int *p declares p as a pointer to int; the * is part of the declarator and does not access memory. A pointer holds an address, so p can be initialized with &value, where & is an address-of operator applied to an existing object. After declaration, p is the pointer, *p is the pointed-to int, and &p is the address of the pointer variable itself (int**). In int *a, b; only a is a pointer. Initialize pointers before dereferencing.
commands.syntax:
int value = 10;
int *p = &value;  // p is int*, * declares it, &value supplies an address
int copy = *p;   // * reads value
*p = 12;        // * writes value

examples.description: Declaration * creates a pointer variable, & obtains an object's address, and expression * accesses the object.

options.description: Declare p as an int pointer; * is declaration syntax, not a read.
Expression yielding the address of value, suitable for initializing p.
The pointer value itself, referring to value after initialization.
Expression referring to the int that p points to.
Address of the pointer variable p; its type is int**.

commands.name: NULL pointer
commands.summary: Represent a pointer not pointing at any object or function.
commands.description: NULL is a null pointer constant macro from headers including stddef.h and stdio.h. Test a pointer before dereferencing when a null value is possible. A null pointer is not necessarily represented by all-zero bytes.

examples.description: Tests allocation before using a pointer.

commands.name: pointer arithmetic
commands.summary: Advance pointers by elements, not bytes.
commands.description: Adding n to a pointer into an array moves n elements. Results may point within the same array or one past its last element; a one-past pointer must not be dereferenced. Subtraction is defined only within one array (subject to representability).

examples.description: Moves two int elements from the first position.

commands.note: Arithmetic on an unrelated pointer is not made valid by casting.

commands.name: pointer to const vs const pointer
commands.summary: Understand which part of a declaration is immutable.
commands.description: const int *p: the pointed-to int cannot be changed through p, but p can change. int *const p: p cannot be reassigned, but *p can change. const int *const p applies both restrictions.

examples.description: Shows the difference between fixed pointer and read-only access.

commands.name: pointer to pointer
commands.summary: Store the address of another pointer.
commands.description: int **pp points to an int* object; *pp is the inner pointer and **pp is the int it designates. This is useful for updating caller pointers or handling arrays of pointers.

examples.description: Two dereferences reach the original integer.

commands.name: void *
commands.summary: Hold a generic object pointer.
commands.description: A void* can receive pointers to object types and convert back. C permits implicit conversion between void* and object pointers. Standard C does not allow dereferencing a void* or doing arithmetic on it directly.

examples.description: Converts a generic object pointer back to its original type.

commands.note: Function pointers are not generally interchangeable with void* under ISO C.

commands.name: malloc
commands.summary: Allocate uninitialized dynamic storage.
commands.description: malloc(size) obtains size bytes of suitably aligned storage, or returns NULL on failure. The bytes are uninitialized; initialize before reading them. Release the storage with free exactly once when no longer needed.

examples.description: Allocates and fills four integers.

commands.note: Avoid relying on the behavior of malloc(0); it is implementation-defined.

commands.name: calloc
commands.summary: Allocate storage initialized to all zero bits.
commands.description: calloc(count, size) allocates space for an array of count elements and sets all bytes to zero. For standard integer types this produces zero values. Check for allocation failure and release the result with free.

examples.description: Allocates three zero-initialized integers.

commands.note: All-bits-zero is not guaranteed to represent a null pointer on every C implementation.

commands.name: realloc
commands.summary: Resize a previously allocated block.
commands.description: realloc may move an allocation. On success the old pointer is invalidated even if the address is unchanged; on failure it returns NULL and leaves the old allocation intact. Preserve the original pointer until success.

examples.description: Uses a temporary pointer to handle realloc failure safely.

options.description: Pointer returned by a previous allocation call, or NULL.

commands.note: Avoid realloc(ptr, 0) in portable code; zero-size behavior differs across C versions and implementations.

commands.name: free
commands.summary: Release dynamically allocated storage.
commands.description: free accepts NULL or a pointer from a compatible allocation function that has not been freed. After free, pointers to the allocation are dangling and must not be dereferenced or freed again.

examples.description: Releases memory and clears the local pointer.

commands.note: Setting one variable to NULL does not clear copies of the pointer elsewhere.

commands.name: memory lifetime and dangling pointers
commands.summary: Know when a pointer stops designating a live object.
commands.description: A pointer becomes invalid for dereference after the pointed-to object ends its lifetime, such as when a local block ends or an allocation is freed. Returning a pointer to a local automatic variable is invalid.

examples.description: Returns a pointer to an object that remains alive in main.

commands.note: Never return &local_variable when local_variable has automatic storage duration.

commands.name: malloc size overflow
commands.summary: Check count times element size before allocating.
commands.description: Multiplying two size_t values can wrap, yielding an allocation smaller than intended. Check count <= SIZE_MAX / sizeof element before computing the byte count.

examples.description: Uses SIZE_MAX from stdint.h to guard multiplication.

commands.name: memcpy
commands.summary: Copy a specified number of bytes between nonoverlapping regions.
commands.description: memcpy(dst, src, n) requires valid storage ranges and must not be used for overlapping regions. Use memmove if the ranges can overlap. The function does not allocate storage or append a string terminator.

examples.description: Copies a complete int array into another of the same type.

commands.name: memmove
commands.summary: Copy bytes safely even when source and destination overlap.
commands.description: memmove behaves as though bytes are first copied into a temporary nonoverlapping buffer. It is useful when moving data within the same array.

examples.description: Shifts four bytes, including the d, to produce aabcd.

commands.note: This example relies on the array having five bytes and does not copy the terminator; the original terminator remains.

commands.name: memset
commands.summary: Set every byte in a memory region to a specified byte value.
commands.description: memset fills bytes; it does not perform typed element assignments. It is useful for clearing character buffers, but an all-zero byte representation is not universally valid for every C type.

examples.description: Clears the bytes of an unsigned char array.

commands.name: memcmp
commands.summary: Compare two memory regions byte by byte.
commands.description: memcmp compares the first n bytes as unsigned char values and returns a negative, zero, or positive integer. It is not a general struct equality test because padding bytes may differ.
commands.syntax: int memcmp(const void *a, const void *b, size_t n);

examples.description: Checks whether the byte sequence a is lexicographically smaller.

commands.note: Do not use memcmp on a struct to compare its logical values.

commands.name: one-dimensional arrays
commands.summary: Store multiple elements of the same type contiguously.
commands.description: Array indices range from 0 to length-1. The compiler does not check out-of-range access automatically. Arrays cannot be assigned as whole objects, though structures containing arrays can be assigned.

examples.description: Declares and iterates through a fixed-size array.

commands.name: multidimensional arrays
commands.summary: Store arrays of arrays in row-major order.
commands.description: int a[2][3] contains two rows, each holding three int elements. In memory the last index varies fastest. For a function taking such an array, all dimensions except the first need to be specified (or supplied as VLA parameters).

examples.description: Reads the final element of a 2-by-3 array.

commands.name: array-to-pointer conversion
commands.summary: Most array expressions become pointers to their first elements.
commands.description: Except in contexts such as sizeof, unary &, and string-literal initialization, an array expression usually converts to a pointer to its first element. A function parameter written int a[] is adjusted to int *a; it does not carry array length.

examples.description: Passes both a pointer and an explicit element count.

commands.note: sizeof on an array parameter measures a pointer, not the original array.

commands.name: variable length arrays (VLA)
commands.summary: Declare an automatic array whose length is computed at runtime (C99).
commands.description: C99 supports variable length arrays in suitable block scopes. Some later C implementations make VLA support optional; large VLAs can exhaust stack space. Validate lengths and prefer heap allocation for large dynamic data.

examples.description: Uses a C99 runtime-sized automatic array.

commands.note: Unlike C++, standard C99 permits VLAs; not every toolchain supports them.

commands.name: C strings and '\0'
commands.summary: Represent text as a sequence of char ending in a null byte.
commands.description: C strings require space for the terminating '\0'. strlen counts characters before the terminator, not buffer capacity. Functions that expect strings need a valid null terminator within accessible storage.

examples.description: The array holds four bytes while the string length is three.

commands.name: strlen
commands.summary: Count bytes before the terminating null character.
commands.description: strlen returns size_t and scans until '\0'. It must be given a valid terminated string; passing a nonterminated byte buffer can read past its bounds.

examples.description: Prints the length excluding the terminator.

commands.note: strlen is not a Unicode character counter.

commands.name: strcmp
commands.summary: Compare two null-terminated strings lexicographically.
commands.description: strcmp returns a negative, zero, or positive integer; do not assume the exact magnitude. It is case-sensitive and compares using unsigned char values.

examples.description: Checks lexicographic ordering without relying on exact return magnitude.

commands.name: strncmp
commands.summary: Compare at most n characters from two C strings.
commands.description: strncmp stops at a difference, a null character, or the limit. Like strcmp it returns a sign, not a guaranteed -1/0/1. It does not solve every problem involving nonterminated byte arrays.
commands.syntax: int strncmp(const char *a, const char *b, size_t n);

examples.description: Compares only the first six characters.

commands.name: strcpy
commands.summary: Copy a C string including its null terminator.
commands.description: strcpy requires the destination to have sufficient space and nonoverlapping storage. The function has no buffer capacity parameter; prefer carefully bounded alternatives when the destination size is not guaranteed.

examples.description: Copies a known short literal into a large enough array.

commands.note: Never use strcpy with an unknown-length source and a fixed destination.

commands.name: strncpy
commands.summary: Copy at most n bytes, with tricky termination behavior.
commands.description: If the source fits before n, strncpy pads the destination with null bytes; otherwise it writes exactly n bytes without adding '\0'. It is not a generally safe drop-in replacement for strcpy.

examples.description: The short source is terminated and padded in this specific example.

commands.note: When truncating, explicitly ensure termination or use a different bounded-copy design.

commands.name: strcat
commands.summary: Append one string to another.
commands.description: strcat finds the destination terminator and writes the source including '\0'. Ensure capacity for the combined strings and prevent overlapping source/destination ranges.

examples.description: Appends when the destination has enough capacity.

options.description: Writable terminated string with spare capacity.

commands.name: strchr
commands.summary: Find the first occurrence of a character in a string.
commands.description: strchr returns a pointer to a matching character or NULL if absent. Searching for '\0' returns a pointer to the terminating null byte.

examples.description: The returned pointer refers to the substring beginning at the first n.

commands.name: strstr
commands.summary: Find the first occurrence of a substring.
commands.description: strstr searches a valid null-terminated haystack for a null-terminated needle. It returns the first match or NULL; the empty needle matches at the start.

examples.description: Finds and prints the matched suffix.

commands.name: strtok
commands.summary: Split a mutable string into tokens using delimiter characters.
commands.description: strtok modifies its input by inserting null terminators and uses internal state across calls. Subsequent calls pass NULL to continue; nested or concurrent tokenization needs a different approach.

examples.description: Splits a mutable comma-separated buffer.

options.description: Mutable input on first call; NULL to continue.

commands.note: strtok skips runs of delimiters and does not return empty fields.

commands.name: ctype.h character tests
commands.summary: Classify and transform single-byte characters.
commands.description: Functions such as isdigit, isalpha, isspace, toupper and tolower require either EOF or an unsigned-char-representable value. Cast potentially negative plain char values to unsigned char before calling.

examples.description: Tests whether a character is a decimal digit.

commands.note: Behavior depends partly on the current locale; ctype functions do not process full Unicode code points.

commands.name: printf
commands.summary: Print formatted text to stdout.
commands.description: printf interprets conversion specifiers. Common ones: %d int, %u unsigned, %f double, %c int character, %s string, %p void pointer, %zu size_t, %lld long long. Argument types must match their specifiers. printf writes to stdout; fprintf selects an explicit stream. Printed values do not change the program's exit status.

examples.description: Prints an integer in decimal and hexadecimal.

commands.note: Return value: number of characters printed on success, or a negative value on output error. This is not a Boolean success value. A type mismatch in a variadic format argument can cause undefined behavior.

commands.name: scanf
commands.summary: Read formatted input from stdin.
commands.description: scanf reads formatted data from stdin; fscanf accepts an explicit FILE* source. For %d pass an int* such as &n. Numeric conversions skip leading whitespace (including newlines), so scanf cannot by itself guarantee exactly one integer per line. Check the return count. Malformed input can leave the offending characters unread; out-of-range conversions to int are not a robust validation method.

examples.description: Tests the conversion count before using the result.

commands.note: Return value: count of successful assignments (possibly 0); EOF if input failure occurs before the first conversion. A successful single %d returns 1, not a general success flag.

commands.name: fgets
commands.summary: Read at most size-1 characters into a buffer.
commands.description: fgets reads at most size - 1 characters from stream into s and adds a terminating '\0'. It stops at a newline (and retains it), end-of-file, or capacity. One call can read only part of a long line: check for a newline and collect the remainder when whole-line validation matters. It does not convert numeric text into int.

examples.description: Reads bounded input, avoiding an unbounded %s conversion.

commands.note: Return value: s (the buffer pointer) on success; NULL if end-of-file occurs before reading any character or on a read error. Inspect feof/ferror if you need to distinguish those cases.

commands.name: puts / fputs
commands.summary: Write a string to stdout or a chosen stream.
commands.description: puts writes the string plus a newline to stdout. fputs writes the string without automatically appending a newline, and accepts a FILE* stream.

examples.description: Contrasts automatic newline handling.

commands.name: getchar / putchar
commands.summary: Read or write a single character.
commands.description: getchar returns an unsigned char converted to int, or EOF on end-of-file/error. Store its result in int rather than char so EOF can be distinguished. putchar writes a character value.

examples.description: Copies one input character if available.

commands.name: EOF and input loops
commands.summary: Distinguish end-of-input from a character or failed conversion.
commands.description: EOF is an integer macro used by many input functions to report end-of-file or a read failure. A failed scanf conversion can return 0 for a nonmatching token, which is different from EOF. fgetc returns an int character value or EOF; inspect feof/ferror after EOF when the distinction matters.

examples.description: Copies input until the stream ends.

commands.note: EOF is a sentinel value, not a function and not a Boolean; feof becomes true only after a read has encountered end-of-file.

commands.name: FILE * streams
commands.summary: Represent open files with the stdio.h stream abstraction.
commands.description: A FILE* is a stream handle used by C standard I/O functions; it is not the file path or the file contents. Hosted C programs already have stdin (input), stdout (normal output), and stderr (diagnostics). Redirection and pipes can connect these streams to files or other programs without changing C code. Reading from a stream advances its position; opening for reading does not modify the file. Close streams you open with fopen.

examples.description: Reads from stdin, sends data to stdout, and sends a separate diagnostic to stderr.

commands.note: FILE* is a type, not a function; a stream has no success/failure return value of its own.

commands.name: fopen
commands.summary: Open a path as a FILE* stream using a mode string.
commands.description: fopen(path, mode) opens a stream attached to a file. With "r" it reads an existing file without changing it; opening alone does not parse any data. "w" immediately creates or truncates a file; "a" creates or appends. A plus sign adds both reading and writing; b requests binary mode (important where text-mode translation occurs). If opening fails, fopen returns NULL; never use that pointer for I/O. Close successfully opened streams with fclose.

examples.description: Open an argument path for reading; fopen returns a stream, then fscanf actually reads from it.

options.description: Path as a null-terminated string (for example argv[1] or "grades.txt").
Read existing file; fail if it cannot be opened.
Create or truncate existing file immediately; write only.
Create if needed; all writes append to the end.
Read and write an existing file; do not truncate.
Read and write; create or truncate immediately.
Read and append; create if needed; all writes go to the end.
Binary variants of r, w, and a; on some systems they avoid text newline translation.
Binary read/write variants; "rb+", "wb+", and "ab+" also work in ISO C.

commands.note: Return value: FILE* on success; NULL on failure. "w" and "w+" erase existing contents upon opening.

commands.name: fclose
commands.summary: Flush and close a FILE* stream.
commands.description: fclose flushes buffered output (if any), closes the stream, and releases its resources. Afterward the FILE* is invalid. Do not fclose a stream that failed to open; a stream opened by fopen should be closed, including on early error paths. Check output-stream closure if write correctness matters.

examples.description: Closes a temporary file and checks for failure.

commands.note: Return value: 0 on success; EOF on failure. Closing stdin, stdout, or stderr is usually unnecessary in a simple program.

commands.name: fprintf / fscanf
commands.summary: Perform formatted I/O with an explicit stream.
commands.description: fprintf writes formatted output to the chosen stream; fscanf reads formatted input from a chosen stream. scanf(format, ...) is equivalent to fscanf(stdin, format, ...) and printf(format, ...) writes to stdout. Use fprintf(stderr, ...) for diagnostics. For fscanf("%d", &value), a matching number produces one successful assignment; malformed tokens may produce zero, and EOF before any conversion produces EOF. fscanf skips whitespace before numeric conversions, not line boundaries.
commands.syntax:
int fprintf(FILE *stream, const char *format, ...);
int fscanf(FILE *stream, const char *format, ...);

examples.description: Checks a single integer conversion and separates normal output from diagnostics.

options.description: A FILE* such as stdin, stdout, stderr, or a stream from fopen.
A format string with matching conversions such as %d for int.
Values for fprintf; writable destination pointers for fscanf.

commands.note: Return values: fprintf returns the number of characters written or a negative value on failure; fscanf returns assignments made (0 is possible), or EOF for input failure before any assignment.

commands.name: snprintf
commands.summary: Format text into a bounded character buffer (C99).
commands.description: snprintf writes at most size bytes, including the terminator if size is nonzero. It returns the number of characters that would have been written, excluding the terminator, or a negative value on encoding error. Detect truncation by comparing with size.
commands.syntax: int snprintf(char *buf, size_t size, const char *fmt, ...);

examples.description: Formats into an array while checking capacity.

commands.name: fread / fwrite
commands.summary: Read or write binary blocks of data.
commands.description: fread and fwrite transfer a number of elements each having a given size. Their return values count complete elements processed. Check ferror and feof to understand short reads; raw binary layouts are often not portable between systems.
commands.syntax:
fread(ptr, size, count, stream)
fwrite(ptr, size, count, stream)

examples.description: Writes and reads raw bytes using a temporary stream.

commands.note: Do not write pointers or padded struct objects to disk expecting cross-platform portability.

commands.name: fseek / ftell / rewind
commands.summary: Change or inspect a stream's file position.
commands.description: fseek uses a long offset and an origin such as SEEK_SET, SEEK_CUR or SEEK_END. ftell reports a position indicator; rewind seeks to the start and clears errors. Text-stream offsets have portability restrictions.

examples.description: Returns to the beginning of a temporary stream.

commands.note: For portable text streams, only use offsets obtained from ftell (and zero) as permitted by the standard.

commands.name: perror / errno
commands.summary: Report error details after a failing library call.
commands.description: After a function reports failure, perror prints a prefix and an error description to stderr based on the current errno. errno is an error-code macro, not a function return value; a nonzero errno alone does not prove the latest operation failed. Not every library failure reports a useful errno; consult the function contract.

examples.description: Reports the reason for an unsuccessful fopen.

commands.note: Return value: perror is void; errno is an error-code value. Check fopen's NULL result before calling perror.

commands.name: designated initializers
commands.summary: Initialize named struct members or selected array indices (C99).
commands.description: Designated initializers improve clarity and allow out-of-order member initialization. Unspecified members receive the same initialization as objects with static storage duration (zero for arithmetic types).

examples.description: Initializes struct members by name.

commands.name: struct padding and alignment
commands.summary: Recognize that fields can have gaps between them.
commands.description: Compilers may insert padding between members and at the end of a struct to satisfy alignment requirements. sizeof(struct) need not equal the sum of member sizes. Use offsetof for member offsets; avoid serializing raw structs for interoperability.

examples.description: Shows the size and member offset without assuming platform-specific results.

commands.name: self-referential linked-node struct
commands.summary: Point from one struct to another of the same type.
commands.description: A struct may contain pointers to its own incomplete type; it cannot directly contain a member of its full type by value because that would require infinite size.
commands.syntax: struct Node { int value; struct Node *next; };

examples.description: Builds a two-node linked structure on the stack.

commands.name: bit-fields
commands.summary: Declare struct members occupying a specified number of bits.
commands.description: Bit-fields can reduce storage for small flags, but layout, alignment, and ordering are implementation-defined. Use unsigned int bit-fields when a known unsigned range is wanted.

examples.description: Stores a one-bit flag in a struct.

commands.note: Do not assume bit-field layout matches a wire format or file format.

commands.name: atoi / strtol
commands.summary: Convert text to integers, preferably with validation.
commands.description: atoi does not provide reliable error reporting. strtol converts the initial integer portion of a string to long; end receives the address of the first unparsed character. Reject end == s (no digits), unexpected trailing characters, and results outside the permitted application range. Set errno = 0 before the call and test errno == ERANGE to detect overflow/underflow. Only cast to int after checking its range. A successful conversion may legitimately return 0.
commands.syntax: long strtol(const char *s, char **end, int base);

examples.description: Validates an entire decimal string and the permitted 0–100 range before converting to int.

options.description: Optional pointer receiving the first unparsed character.

commands.note: Return values: strtol returns the converted long, or LONG_MAX/LONG_MIN for range overflow with errno == ERANGE; atoi returns an int but offers no dependable error check. strtol does not return 1 for success.

commands.name: strtod
commands.summary: Convert text to double with error reporting.
commands.description: strtod parses a floating-point number and reports the stopping point through endptr. Range errors may set errno to ERANGE. Check both parser progress and trailing content.

examples.description: Parses a simple double and verifies full consumption.

commands.name: abs / labs / llabs
commands.summary: Return an integer's absolute value.
commands.description: abs accepts int, labs long, and llabs long long. If the positive value is not representable (for example abs(INT_MIN) in ordinary two's-complement int), behavior is undefined.

examples.description: Finds absolute value for a representable result.

commands.note: abs(INT_MIN) can overflow; handle the minimum signed value separately.

commands.name: math.h: sqrt / pow / fabs
commands.summary: Use standard mathematical functions.
commands.description: sqrt computes a square root, pow raises to a power, and fabs returns floating absolute value. Many math operations are approximate and may set errno or raise floating exceptions on domain/range errors.
commands.syntax:
double sqrt(double x);
double pow(double x, double y);

examples.description: Uses math.h functions on double values.

commands.note: On some Unix toolchains you must link the math library using -lm.

commands.name: rand / srand
commands.summary: Generate pseudorandom integers from an implementation-defined sequence.
commands.description: rand returns an integer between 0 and RAND_MAX. Call srand to choose a seed. Quality and range vary by implementation; rand is not suitable for cryptography. rand() % n can be biased.

examples.description: Seeds and reads a pseudorandom value.

commands.note: Use a dedicated random source for security-sensitive tokens and keys.

commands.name: qsort
commands.summary: Sort an array using a comparison callback.
commands.description: qsort sorts fixed-size elements in place. Its comparator receives const void* pointers to two elements and must return a negative, zero, or positive int. Use a comparison that does not overflow and does not mutate array elements.
commands.syntax: void qsort(void *base, size_t n, size_t size, int (*cmp)(const void *, const void *));

examples.description: Sorts integers using a safe three-way comparator.

commands.note: qsort is not guaranteed to be stable; do not use return x - y when subtraction can overflow.

commands.name: bsearch
commands.summary: Binary-search a sorted array with a comparator.
commands.description: bsearch requires an array sorted according to the same comparator. It returns a pointer to a matching element or NULL; if several compare equal, which one is returned is unspecified.
commands.syntax: void *bsearch(const void *key, const void *base, size_t n, size_t size, int (*cmp)(const void *, const void *));

examples.description: Searches a sorted array for 5.

commands.name: exit / EXIT_SUCCESS / EXIT_FAILURE
commands.summary: Terminate a hosted program with a status code.
commands.description: exit performs normal termination, including calling registered atexit handlers and flushing/closing standard streams as specified. A return from main also causes normal termination. EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE are portable symbolic statuses.

examples.description: Returns a named portable success code.

commands.name: assert
commands.summary: Check an assumption during development.
commands.description: assert(condition) writes a diagnostic and aborts if the expression is false when assertions are enabled. Defining NDEBUG before including assert.h disables checks; do not put required side effects inside assert.

examples.description: Documents an internal invariant that should always hold.

commands.note: Use ordinary runtime validation for recoverable user-input errors.

commands.name: time / clock
commands.summary: Measure calendar time or approximate processor time.
commands.description: time returns calendar time in seconds when representable by time_t. clock returns an approximation of processor time, converted to seconds by dividing by CLOCKS_PER_SEC. Neither guarantees high-resolution wall-clock timing.
commands.syntax:
time_t now = time(NULL);
clock_t start = clock();

examples.description: Checks whether calendar time was obtained.

commands.name: limits.h / float.h
commands.summary: Inspect implementation-specific numeric limits.
commands.description: limits.h provides integer bounds such as INT_MAX, LONG_MIN, CHAR_BIT. float.h exposes properties such as DBL_MAX and DBL_EPSILON. Use these instead of assuming machine widths or floating precision.

examples.description: Prints limits from the actual implementation.

commands.name: NULL / offsetof / ptrdiff_t (stddef.h)
commands.summary: Use core size, pointer-difference, and offset definitions.
commands.description: stddef.h defines size_t, ptrdiff_t, NULL and offsetof. offsetof measures the byte offset of a structure member from its start. Some headers supply the types independently.

examples.description: Shows a standard layout offset query.

commands.name: setjmp / longjmp
commands.summary: Jump back to a saved execution environment.
commands.description: setjmp saves a calling environment to a jmp_buf; longjmp transfers control back. This mechanism is specialized and interacts with local non-volatile variables and resource cleanup. Prefer ordinary error returns for most applications.

examples.description: Demonstrates a jump to a saved valid environment.

commands.note: Do not jump into a function that has already returned.

commands.name: gcc compile command
commands.summary: Compile and link C99 source code with warnings.
commands.description: gcc -std=c99 selects the C99 language mode; -Wall and -Wextra enable many useful diagnostics. -o chooses an output filename. Compiling is separate from executing the resulting binary.

examples.description: A complete source file and shell commands to build and run it.

commands.note: Warnings are valuable even when compilation succeeds.

commands.name: separate compilation and headers
commands.summary: Compile multiple C files into one program.
commands.description: A common design places public declarations in .h files and definitions in .c files. Each .c file becomes a translation unit. Include guards prevent duplicate processing, while the linker combines the object files.
commands.syntax:
gcc -c module.c
gcc main.o module.o -o program

examples.description: Shows a function declaration and a second translation unit layout.

commands.note: The example illustrates two files; compile them separately using the commands in Syntax.

commands.name: Makefile basics
commands.summary: Define reproducible compilation targets and dependencies.
commands.description: make updates targets whose prerequisites are newer. Recipe lines normally begin with a tab character. A Makefile helps keep compilation options and multi-file dependencies consistent.
commands.syntax:
CC = gcc
CFLAGS = -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra
program: main.c
	$(CC) $(CFLAGS) main.c -o program

examples.description: Use the Makefile syntax in the Syntax field to build main.c.

commands.name: compiler warnings and sanitizers
commands.summary: Catch mistakes before and during execution.
commands.description: Use -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic for additional compile-time checks. On supporting GCC/Clang platforms, -fsanitize=address,undefined helps detect many runtime errors. Sanitizers do not prove a program is correct.

examples.description: Uses warnings, debug symbols, and runtime instrumentation.

commands.note: Availability and specific diagnostics depend on the compiler/runtime.

commands.name: gdb debugging basics
commands.summary: Inspect a compiled C program step by step.
commands.description: Compile with -g to include debug symbols. In gdb, use break main, run, next, step, print variable, backtrace, and continue. Debugger commands are not C language statements.

examples.description: A small program whose variables can be inspected in a debugger.

commands.name: undefined vs unspecified vs implementation-defined
commands.summary: Recognize three different portability classifications.
commands.description: Undefined behavior gives no requirements on the program's outcome. Unspecified behavior allows several documented possibilities without requiring which one is chosen. Implementation-defined behavior requires the implementation to document its selected behavior.

examples.description: A fully defined alternative to reading outside an array.

commands.note: Examples of UB include signed overflow, invalid pointer dereference, and unsequenced modifications.

commands.name: header guards
commands.summary: Prevent a header's declarations from being processed more than once.
commands.description: A common pattern is #ifndef NAME_H / #define NAME_H / ... / #endif. Choose unique guard identifiers. #pragma once is widely supported but not standardized by C99.

examples.description: Illustrates a conventional portable header guard.

commands.name: const void * in callbacks
commands.summary: Read a qsort comparator's pointer levels correctly.
commands.description: A qsort comparator receives pointers to array elements. For an array of int*, each element has type int*, so each comparator argument points to an int*: cast to int *const * (or const int *const * only when the original pointed-to objects have compatible qualification), then dereference twice to read an int.

examples.description: Correctly sorts pointers by their referenced integer values.

commands.note: int *const * describes a pointer to a const pointer to int; it does not make the pointed-to int const.

commands.name: const correctness across function parameters
commands.summary: Express when a function promises not to modify an object.
commands.description: const int *p prevents modification of *p through p. For arrays passed as pointers, const documents read-only access. A pointer parameter itself is still passed by value and can be reassigned locally.

examples.description: Uses const to express a read-only pointer parameter.

commands.name: fgetc / fputc
commands.summary: Read and write individual characters from/to a FILE stream.
commands.description: fgetc reads one byte/character from a FILE* stream and returns it as an unsigned char converted to int; it returns EOF on end-of-file or error. Use int rather than char for the result so EOF remains distinguishable. fputc writes a character to a stream.
commands.syntax:
int fgetc(FILE *stream);
int fputc(int c, FILE *stream);

examples.description: Writes and reads one character from a temporary stream.

commands.note: Return values: fgetc returns a character value or EOF; fputc returns the character written (as unsigned char converted to int) or EOF on error.

commands.name: feof / ferror / clearerr
commands.summary: Inspect and reset stream error and end-of-file indicators.
commands.description: feof reports whether the stream's end-of-file indicator was set by an earlier read; ferror reports the error indicator. Both return nonzero if set and zero otherwise. clearerr resets both indicators and returns no value; they cannot predict the next read's outcome.

examples.description: Distinguishes stream EOF from an I/O error.

commands.note: Return values: feof/ferror return nonzero when their respective indicator is set, otherwise 0; clearerr returns void. Do not loop on !feof: test each read instead.

commands.name: restrict pointer
commands.summary: Promise restricted aliasing for certain pointer accesses (C99).
commands.description: restrict is an optimization contract for access through suitably designated pointers. Violating it may cause undefined behavior. Use only when the function's aliasing requirements can really be guaranteed.
commands.syntax: void add(size_t n, int *restrict a, const int *restrict b);

examples.description: Adds disjoint arrays with a restrict-qualified destination.

commands.note: Passing overlapping arrays may violate the restrict contract.

commands.name: _Generic selection
commands.summary: Choose an expression according to its type (C11).
commands.description: A _Generic selection matches a controlling expression's type against associations at compile time. It provides type-based dispatch without runtime inspection and is available in C11 and later.

examples.description: Compile with -std=c11; matches an int expression.

commands.note: Not available in strict C99.

commands.name: floating-point special values
commands.summary: Understand NaN, infinities, and comparison behavior.
commands.description: On implementations supporting IEC 60559-style floating point, NaN is unordered and comparisons with it (except !=) are false. INFINITY and NAN macros may be available from math.h depending on the implementation. Do not rely on exact IEEE representation without checking.

examples.description: Checks whether an ordinary floating-point value is finite.

commands.note: Availability and behavior of infinities/NaNs depend on the floating-point implementation.

commands.name: string formatting and precision
commands.summary: Control alignment, width, and precision in printf.
commands.description: A field width specifies minimum output width; a precision for %f specifies digits after the decimal point, and for %s limits bytes printed. Width/precision do not make an incorrect format argument type safe.

examples.description: Formats a number with padding and limits the printed prefix of a string.

commands.name: scanf field widths
commands.summary: Bound string conversions and check assignment counts.
commands.description: For a char buffer with capacity 10, %9s leaves room for the terminating '\0'. %c does not append a terminator. A field width for %s does not prevent all logical input errors; prefer fgets plus parsing for complex input.

examples.description: Bounds a %s conversion to nine characters.

commands.note: A field width is a maximum conversion width, not a guarantee that input is valid.

commands.name: array of pointers
commands.summary: Store pointers as elements rather than storing values directly.
commands.description: int *items[3] is an array of three pointers to int. This differs from int (*p)[3], which is a pointer to an array of three int values. The parentheses change the declarator's meaning.

examples.description: Reads an integer through an array element that is itself a pointer.

commands.name: pointer to array
commands.summary: Point at a whole fixed-size array.
commands.description: int (*p)[3] is a pointer to an array of three ints. Incrementing p advances by three integers, not one. Contrast int *p[3], an array of pointers.

examples.description: Uses a pointer whose pointed-to object is the entire array.

commands.name: const array data and string literals
commands.summary: Avoid attempting to modify literal text.
commands.description: A string literal has array-of-char type in C, but trying to modify it is undefined behavior. A char array initialized from a string literal creates separate writable storage; const char * is often the correct type for a read-only string parameter.

examples.description: Only the char array copy is modified.

commands.name: integer division and negative remainder
commands.summary: Remember truncation toward zero for signed integer division.
commands.description: For C99 and later, division of integers discards the fractional part toward zero; the remainder has the sign of the dividend (or is zero). a == (a / b) * b + (a % b) when defined.

examples.description: Prints -2 and -1 under C99 division rules.

commands.note: INT_MIN / -1 can be undefined when the quotient is not representable.

commands.name: main arguments: argc and argv
commands.summary: Receive command-line arguments in a hosted program.
commands.description: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) receives a count and an array of argument strings. On usual command-line launches argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] the first argument, and argc includes the program name. Check argc before accessing argv[1]; absent arguments do not imply an empty argv[1]. argv[argc] is NULL. Filenames and relative or absolute paths are ordinary strings, not file handles.

examples.description: Run as ./program data/grades.txt or ./program; check argc before argv[1].

commands.note: The result returned by main is a program exit status, not a function input conversion count: return 0 indicates success; return EXIT_FAILURE (from stdlib.h) indicates failure portably.

commands.name: stdin / stdout / stderr
commands.summary: Use the three pre-opened standard C streams.
commands.description: Hosted C programs start with stdin for input, stdout for ordinary output, and stderr for diagnostics. scanf and getchar read stdin; printf and putchar write stdout; fprintf(stderr, ...) writes diagnostics. In a shell, redirection and pipelines connect these streams to a terminal, file, or another program. C's stream names designate FILE* handles, not paths or text stored in strings.

examples.description: Run with a terminal, ./program < data.txt, or printf '42\n' | ./program; C always reads from stdin.

commands.note: A stream does not itself return 0 or 1. Individual I/O calls have distinct return contracts, and main's exit status is separate from stderr output.

topics.name: Getting started with C99
topics.summary: Create, build, and run a first C program.
topics.description: C is a compiled language; write source, compile it, review diagnostics, and run the executable separately.

sections.title: Minimal program
sections.body: A hosted C program starts in main. Include only the headers required by the functions you use.

sections.title: Compile and execute
sections.body: Save source as hello.c, run gcc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra hello.c -o hello, then run ./hello on a Unix-like system.

sections.title: Common beginner mistakes
sections.body: A missing semicolon, calling undeclared functions, type-mismatched format specifiers, and confusing source files with executables are frequent early errors.

examples.description: A complete program that can be compiled with a C99 compiler.

topics.name: Variables, types, and initialization
topics.summary: Choose types and initialize every value before reading.
topics.description: C is statically typed, and object declarations determine representation, allowed operations, storage duration, and visibility.

sections.title: Choose a suitable type
sections.body: Use int for ordinary integers, size_t for sizes, double for fractional calculations, and char arrays or pointers for text. Use stdint.h when explicit widths are truly required.

sections.title: Initialize before use
sections.body: An automatic scalar without an initializer generally has an indeterminate value. Reading such a value may have undefined behavior.

sections.title: Conversions and casts
sections.body: Integer promotions and usual arithmetic conversions can affect comparisons and calculations; add explicit casts only where meaningful.

sections.title: Ranges and portability
sections.body: Read limits.h and float.h rather than assuming all platforms use identical type widths.

examples.description: Combines initialized variables with correctly typed division.

topics.name: Expressions, evaluation, and precedence
topics.summary: Understand what an expression computes and when side effects occur.
topics.description: Parsing order and runtime evaluation order are different; parenthesizing clarifies grouping but cannot make all side effects safe.

sections.title: Grouping
sections.body: Multiplication binds tighter than addition; unary operators usually bind tighter than binary arithmetic. Use parentheses when the intended grouping is not obvious.

sections.title: Evaluation order
sections.body: Function-call arguments and many operands are evaluated in an unspecified order; do not use expressions that require a particular ordering.

sections.title: Short circuit
sections.body: && and || conditionally skip the right operand and are suitable for guarding pointer access.

sections.title: Overflow and division
sections.body: Signed integer overflow and division by zero are undefined. Integer division truncates toward zero in C99.

examples.description: Combines grouping and a safely guarded division.

topics.name: Conditionals and loops
topics.summary: Select paths and repeat operations without infinite loops.
topics.description: Use if/else for arbitrary conditions, switch for integral labels, and for/while/do-while for iteration.

sections.title: if and switch
sections.body: Use if for range or compound conditions. switch selects labels and needs explicit break to prevent unintended fallthrough.

sections.title: for, while and do-while
sections.body: for is convenient for counted iteration; while checks before the body; do-while checks after and therefore runs at least once.

sections.title: Break and continue
sections.body: break exits the nearest loop/switch, while continue moves to the next loop iteration.

sections.title: Loop invariants and bounds
sections.body: Be precise about start, stopping condition, increment, and whether n is included. Use size_t when indexing with nonnegative array sizes.

examples.description: A counted loop computes the sum 1 through 5.

topics.name: Functions, prototypes, and separate files
topics.summary: Write reusable functions with predictable interfaces.
topics.description: Function prototypes provide type checking, while definitions provide implementation. C uses call-by-value even when the parameter's value is a pointer.

sections.title: Prototype before call
sections.body: A prototype such as int add(int a, int b); can appear in a header or before main.

sections.title: Parameters and return values
sections.body: Function parameters are local copies of argument values. Pass a pointer to modify caller-owned data.

sections.title: Scope and linkage
sections.body: static at file scope limits linkage to one translation unit; extern declarations can refer to an externally linked definition.

sections.title: Headers
sections.body: Use include guards; include declarations and relevant type definitions, not non-inline ordinary function definitions in shared headers.

examples.description: Declares a function first, then defines it after main.

topics.name: Pointers from first principles
topics.summary: Build a reliable mental model of addresses and indirection.
topics.description: A pointer stores a value that may designate an object or function; the pointer variable and the pointed-to object are distinct.

sections.title: Declaration versus expression
sections.body: In int *p = &x;, the * belongs to the declaration and says p has type int*. The &x is an expression that produces x's address. Later *p is an expression that reads or changes x. &p instead produces the address of the pointer variable p (type int**).

sections.title: Which operator do you need?
sections.body: To obtain an object's address, use &x. To use the object through a pointer, use *p. To pass an int variable to scanf("%d", &x), use &x because scanf needs an int*; to print the value through an initialized pointer, use printf("%d", *p).

sections.title: Indirection levels
sections.body: int **pp points to an int* object; *pp is a pointer, **pp an int. Count dereferences according to the pointed-to layers.

sections.title: Null and invalid pointers
sections.body: NULL designates no object. Do not dereference NULL, dangling, or one-past-end pointers.

sections.title: Pointer arithmetic
sections.body: Adding n to int* advances by n int elements within one array; pointer subtraction yields element counts.

sections.title: Const placement
sections.body: const int *p restricts writes through p; int *const p fixes the address stored in p.

examples.description: Shows a value, pointer, and pointer to pointer working together.

topics.name: Reading complex C declarators
topics.summary: Decode pointers, arrays, functions, and const placement.
topics.description: Read outward from the declared identifier while respecting parentheses and postfix []/() binding more tightly than prefix *.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body: int *a[3] means an array of three int pointers; int (*p)[3] means a pointer to an array of three int. Parentheses change the type.

sections.title: Const pointer
sections.body: int *const p is a fixed pointer to writable int. const int *p is a reassignable pointer through which int cannot be modified.

sections.title: Comparator cast
sections.body: With int *array[], each qsort element is int*. const void* comparator parameters point to those elements; int *const * expresses a pointer to a const pointer to int.

sections.title: Function pointer
sections.body: int (*f)(int) is a pointer to a function taking int and returning int.

examples.description: An array of pointers viewed through a pointer-to-const-pointer.

topics.name: Arrays, dimensions, and memory layout
topics.summary: Understand array elements, row-major storage, and parameter adjustment.
topics.description: An array is a contiguous collection of elements; many expressions convert an array to a pointer, but an array object is not itself a pointer variable.

sections.title: One dimension
sections.body: Use sizeof a / sizeof a[0] for a local fixed array with known complete array type.

sections.title: Two dimensions
sections.body: For int m[2][3], the last index changes fastest. m[1][0] follows m[0][2] in row-major order.

sections.title: Function parameters
