sections.body: A parameter written int a[] is adjusted to int*. Pass the length separately.

sections.title: Different pointer types
sections.body: int *a[3] is an array of pointers; int (*p)[3] points to an entire 3-element array.

examples.description: Visits all elements in row-major order.

topics.name: Strings and safe text processing
topics.summary: Work with null-terminated char sequences without overflows.
topics.description: C strings are byte arrays terminated by '\0'. APIs require valid capacities and terminators; strings are not automatically length-checked.

sections.title: Capacity versus length
sections.body: sizeof local_array yields its byte size, while strlen counts bytes before the first '\0'. For char s[]="abc", sizeof s is 4 and strlen(s) is 3.

sections.title: Input
sections.body: Use fgets to bound input size. scanf %s must have an appropriate field width.

sections.title: Copying and appending
sections.body: strcpy/strcat require enough destination space and nonoverlap. snprintf is useful for bounded formatting.

sections.title: Comparing
sections.body: strcmp returns only a sign. Never compare C strings using pointer equality if you want their text compared.

sections.title: Encoding
sections.body: strlen counts bytes, not necessarily Unicode characters.

examples.description: Demonstrates string length and a terminated char array.

topics.name: Dynamic memory and ownership
topics.summary: Allocate, resize, and free memory without leaks or invalid access.
topics.description: Dynamic storage uses malloc/calloc/realloc and must be released with free. Track which code owns each allocation and how long references stay valid.

sections.title: Allocate safely
sections.body: Use malloc(count * sizeof *p), check against NULL, and protect multiplication from overflow for untrusted counts.

sections.title: Initialize
sections.body: malloc leaves bytes uninitialized; calloc zeros bytes; explicit typed assignment is still needed for some representations.

sections.title: Resize
sections.body: Use tmp = realloc(p, newsize); update p only after success. On failure the old allocation remains valid.

sections.title: Release once
sections.body: free exactly once when the object is no longer needed. Never dereference a pointer after its allocation is freed.

sections.title: Borrowing
sections.body: A pointer returned by a function does not automatically imply ownership. Define who frees memory in your API.

examples.description: Allocates, initializes, uses, and releases a dynamic array.

topics.name: Formatted input and robust parsing
topics.summary: Understand conversion counts, EOF, and text-to-number alternatives.
topics.description: Formatted input may fail because of end-of-file, bad syntax, or range issues. Treat return values as part of the API contract.

sections.title: scanf return value
sections.body: scanf returns the number of successful assignments. An invalid token can produce 0; EOF before any conversion reports EOF.

sections.title: Whitespace
sections.body: Most numeric scanf conversions skip leading whitespace; newline alone does not signal end-of-input.

sections.title: Read then parse
sections.body: Read a complete line first if errors must cite its original text or exactly one integer per line is required. strtol gives a long, an end pointer, and ERANGE for range overflow; check the entire line and application range before converting to int. A fixed-size fgets buffer can split a long invalid line.

sections.title: Format matching
sections.body: In scanf, %f expects float* and %lf expects double*. In printf, %f expects double due to default promotions.

examples.description: Demonstrates bounded input and partial integer parsing; it does not yet reject trailing text or long split lines.

topics.name: Files, streams, and error handling
topics.summary: Open, read, write, and close files defensively.
topics.description: stdio.h abstracts buffered I/O through FILE*. A good program checks every operation whose failure matters and closes resources on all paths.

sections.title: Open modes
sections.body: fopen mode strings: r read existing; w create/truncate immediately; a create/append; r+ read/write existing; w+ read/write with truncation; a+ read/append. Append b for binary mode (for example rb or w+b). These are mode strings, not command-line flags.

sections.title: Return values
sections.body: Return conventions differ: fopen gives FILE* or NULL; fgets gives its destination pointer or NULL; fprintf gives characters written or a negative error value; fscanf gives assignment count, 0 for matching failure, or EOF for input failure before conversion; fclose gives 0 or EOF.

sections.title: EOF versus error
sections.body: After an unsuccessful read, feof and ferror distinguish end-of-file from a stream error.

sections.title: Positioning
sections.body: Use fseek/ftell carefully; binary and text streams have different portable offset rules.

sections.title: Cleanup
sections.body: fclose even on error paths. Check fclose when it matters whether buffered output was fully committed.

examples.description: Creates a text file with basic failure checks.

topics.name: Structures, unions, and enumeration
topics.summary: Model grouped records, overlapping storage, and named states.
topics.description: struct groups fields, union overlays members, and enum defines integer constant names; their layout and semantics are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Structures
sections.body: Members have individual storage and may have padding. A struct value can be copied by assignment.

sections.title: Unions
sections.body: Members share storage; writing one member does not automatically convert a different member's value.

sections.title: Enums
sections.body: Useful for named state values; C enumeration types are related to integer types, not scoped classes as in C++.

sections.title: Linked structures
sections.body: A struct can contain a pointer to itself, enabling lists and trees.

sections.title: Layout portability
sections.body: Use offsetof and sizeof to observe your implementation's layout rather than hard-coding assumptions.

examples.description: Combines a struct with an enum state.

topics.name: The preprocessor and header design
topics.summary: Separate text substitution from the C compiler's type system.
topics.description: Preprocessing handles includes, conditional compilation, and macros before normal C compilation; macro substitution is not the same as a typed function call.

sections.title: Headers
sections.body: Place declarations and types needed by multiple source files in headers. Add unique include guards.

sections.title: Macros
sections.body: #define substitutes preprocessing tokens. Parenthesize expression parameters and avoid evaluating argument expressions more than once.

sections.title: Conditional compilation
sections.body: #if and #ifdef select code at compile time; this is distinct from runtime if.

sections.title: Standard features
sections.body: Use library functions and const/enum for many tasks rather than reaching for a function-like macro.

examples.description: Defines a simple object-like macro.

topics.name: Sorting, searching, and callbacks
topics.summary: Use library algorithms with correct pointer levels.
topics.description: qsort and bsearch work on arbitrary fixed-size array elements through void pointers, which makes comparator types important.

sections.title: Comparator contract
sections.body: Return a negative int when first < second, zero when equal, and positive when first > second. Do not assume exact -1 or +1 is required.

sections.title: Elements versus values
sections.body: The comparator gets pointers to array elements. With an int array, cast to const int*. With an int* array, each element is a pointer, so a pointer-to-pointer type is needed.

sections.title: Overflow-safe compare
sections.body: Use (x > y) - (x < y), not x - y when the latter could overflow.

sections.title: Binary search
sections.body: bsearch requires data sorted according to the exact same comparison order.

sections.title: Stability
sections.body: qsort does not promise to preserve the order of equal elements.

examples.description: Sorts an array of actual int values.

topics.name: Undefined behavior and common C pitfalls
topics.summary: Learn why compiling successfully does not guarantee correct execution.
topics.description: The C standard leaves certain incorrect programs with undefined behavior; compilers may optimize assuming those situations do not occur.

sections.title: Out-of-bounds access
sections.body: Only dereference array elements within their valid range. One-past-end pointers may be formed but not dereferenced.

sections.title: Use after lifetime
sections.body: A pointer to a local variable is invalid after that object's lifetime ends; freed allocation references also become invalid.

sections.title: Uninitialized data
sections.body: Read automatic scalars only after initialization.

sections.title: Arithmetic
sections.body: Signed overflow and division by zero have undefined behavior; shift counts also have strict bounds.

sections.title: Sequencing
sections.body: Avoid expressions that modify an object more than once without sequencing.

sections.title: Formats
sections.body: Use printf/scanf specifiers matching the actual argument types.

examples.description: Uses a bounded traversal that avoids invalid array accesses.

topics.name: C99 compilation and debugging workflow
topics.summary: Build reproducibly, observe warnings, and diagnose runtime errors.
topics.description: A simple debug loop is compile with warnings and symbols, run small tests, inspect failures, and use a debugger or sanitizer when appropriate.

sections.title: Compile
sections.body: gcc -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -g source.c -o program checks common issues while adding debug symbols.

sections.title: Link
sections.body: Missing symbol errors during linking differ from compile errors; include all translation units and required libraries.

sections.title: Debug
sections.body: Use breakpoints and inspect local variables with gdb, or use IDE debugger controls.

sections.title: Runtime tools
sections.body: On supported platforms compile with -fsanitize=address,undefined to detect many memory and undefined-behavior errors.

sections.title: Input/output tests
sections.body: Use files and diff to compare expected output with actual output; trailing spaces and extra newlines may matter in automated grading.

examples.description: A deterministic program suitable for compiling and comparing with expected output.

topics.name: C versus C++: key distinctions
topics.summary: Do not assume a C code example obeys the same rules in C++.
topics.description: Although C and C++ share much syntax, they are separate languages with different type, library, compilation, and feature rules. Entries in this release target ISO C99 unless qualified otherwise.

sections.title: Language mode
sections.body: Compile C files with a C compiler and explicitly request -std=c99 when learning C99. A C++ compiler is not a C compiler.

sections.title: void pointer conversions
sections.body: C implicitly converts void* to object pointers; standard C++ requires an explicit conversion.

sections.title: Boolean and string literals
sections.body: In C99 bool comes from stdbool.h, and ordinary character constants have type int. Literal types and bool handling differ from C++.

sections.title: Advanced features
sections.body: C++ classes, templates, references, overloaded functions, new/delete, std::vector, and iostream are not C99 facilities.

sections.title: Shared interface
sections.body: A public header can sometimes support both languages using extern "C" guards under __cplusplus, but this is not a requirement for ordinary C projects.

examples.description: A valid ISO C99 Boolean example; not a C++ reference.

topics.name: Memory representation and bytes
topics.summary: Use sizeof, alignment, and byte operations without unsafe assumptions.
topics.description: A C byte is the size of char; CHAR_BIT gives its bit width. Object representations, padding, alignment, and endianness can vary by implementation.

sections.title: Sizes
sections.body: sizeof measures bytes, not bits. For bit counts multiply by CHAR_BIT where needed.

sections.title: Representation
sections.body: C does not require every multi-byte object to have the same byte order or padding rules.

sections.title: Copying
sections.body: memcpy and memmove operate on byte representations; they do not convert numeric values.

sections.title: Alignment
sections.body: malloc provides storage suitable for objects with fundamental alignment requirements. Casting an arbitrary byte address to a stricter pointer type is not automatically safe.

sections.title: Serialization
sections.body: Prefer explicit byte formats for files or networks instead of writing raw struct layouts.

examples.description: Reports implementation-specific object representation characteristics.

topics.name: Error handling and cleanup patterns
topics.summary: Check return values and centralize cleanup for complex operations.
topics.description: C programs commonly report errors through return codes, NULL pointers, and errno. Resource ownership should remain explicit, especially across several early-exit paths.

sections.title: Check immediately
sections.body: After malloc or fopen, check for NULL. After scanf, validate the assignment count. Do not assume success.

sections.title: Avoid leaks
sections.body: If later work fails, free allocations and close streams already obtained.

sections.title: Dedicated cleanup
sections.body: For several owned resources, a single cleanup label can simplify all exit paths; using goto for this narrow purpose is common in C.

sections.title: Preserve diagnostics
sections.body: Check the function's documented error mechanism; errno need not be meaningful unless an operation reports failure.

examples.description: Uses a cleanup label to guarantee fclose on both paths.

topics.name: Standard headers map
topics.summary: Find the header that declares the function or type you need.
topics.description: Headers group related C library interfaces. Include the appropriate header rather than relying on incidental transitive declarations.

sections.title: stdio.h
sections.body: printf, scanf, fgets, FILE, fopen, fclose, EOF.

sections.title: stdlib.h
sections.body: malloc, calloc, realloc, free, qsort, bsearch, strtol, exit.

sections.title: string.h
sections.body: strlen, strcmp, strcpy, strstr, memcpy, memmove, memset.

sections.title: stddef.h / stdint.h
sections.body: size_t, ptrdiff_t, offsetof, NULL; fixed-width or minimum-width integer types.

sections.title: ctype.h / math.h
sections.body: Character classification and transformations; floating math such as sqrt, fabs and pow.

sections.title: limits.h / float.h
sections.body: Implementation's integer and floating-point limits.

sections.title: assert.h / errno.h / time.h
sections.body: Assertions, error macros, and clock/calendar-time facilities.

examples.description: Combines declarations from three relevant headers.

topics.name: Complex input, bounds, and output formatting
topics.summary: Avoid fragile scanf loops and output mismatches.
topics.description: Read input with explicit bounds, check conversion results, and generate exact output without accidental separators.

sections.title: Bounded input
sections.body: If a fixed buffer holds N bytes, reserve a byte for the null terminator when reading text.

sections.title: EOF loops
sections.body: A numeric scanf loop stops on nonnumeric input (return 0) or EOF, not necessarily at a newline.

sections.title: Whitespace
sections.body: scanf numeric conversions skip leading whitespace; fgets preserves a newline when it fits.

sections.title: Exact output
sections.body: Automated graders can reject trailing spaces, missing separators, or extra lines. Format separators deliberately.

sections.title: Type-sensitive specifiers
sections.body: Match %d with int, %zu with size_t, %lld with long long, and use & for scanf destinations.

examples.description: Prints exactly one space between values and no trailing space.

topics.name: Practical code review checklist
topics.summary: Check correctness, portability, diagnostics, and cleanup before sharing.
topics.description: Small systematic checks are often more useful than adding features when learning C.

sections.title: Types and initialization
sections.body: Does each variable have the right type? Are automatic values initialized before use?

sections.title: Bounds and lifetimes
sections.body: Are array indices valid? Do all pointers designate live storage? Are dynamically allocated objects freed once?

sections.title: Input errors
sections.body: Are scanf/fgets/strtol results checked? Are input buffers correctly sized?

sections.title: Output
sections.body: Do format specifiers match the argument types? Are required newlines and separators exact?

sections.title: Portability
sections.body: Are language-version assumptions stated and implementation-dependent widths avoided?

sections.title: Build
sections.body: Does the program compile with -std=c99 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic? Are warnings understood rather than ignored?

examples.description: A small complete program suitable for a checklist pass.

topics.name: Use a file path argument or standard input
topics.summary: Read through one FILE* regardless of how input was supplied.
topics.description: A command-line path argument identifies a file to open. With no path argument, stdin already supplies the input data; it need not contain another filename. A relative name such as grades.txt is also a path. The program may be run as ./program grades.txt or ./program < grades.txt.

sections.title: Choose the source
sections.body: Check argc before accessing argv[1]. If a path is present, fopen(argv[1], "r") returns a FILE* on success or NULL on failure. If no argument is present, use stdin directly.

sections.title: Read through one handle
sections.body: Keep the chosen FILE* in input, then use fgets(input) or fscanf(input, ...). fopen only opens the stream: it does not parse or print file contents.

sections.title: Ownership
sections.body: Close streams you opened with fopen. An ordinary program need not close stdin itself. Report errors with fprintf(stderr, ...) or perror after a failed fopen.

sections.title: Shell invocation
sections.body: ./program data/grades.txt passes a path in argv[1]. ./program < data/grades.txt puts file CONTENTS into stdin; ./program without redirection usually reads terminal input.

examples.description: Illustrates the source-selection pattern for already-valid whitespace-separated integers; use line-based parsing to validate one value per line.

topics.name: Validate one integer per input line
topics.summary: Preserve original text, validate a complete line, and then use an int.
topics.description: When error messages must include the original line and input must contain exactly one valid integer per line, read a whole line as text first. A C99 int of four bytes does not bound the length of a malformed line. A fixed-size fgets buffer may split a long line; collect additional chunks or grow a buffer with realloc when full input must be retained.

sections.title: Read the whole line
sections.body: fgets reads at most capacity minus one characters; a retained newline indicates completion except on a final line without newline. fgetc with a growable buffer can support arbitrary finite line lengths using ISO C99; getline is POSIX, not ISO C99.

sections.title: Parse without losing the text
sections.body: strtol(line, &end, 10) gives a long and points end to the first unparsed character. Check end != line, errno != ERANGE, and that only permitted whitespace remains. scanf("%d", ...) skips whitespace across line boundaries and cannot preserve malformed line text by itself.

sections.title: Validate before conversion
sections.body: Reject values outside the application's allowed range before casting to int. For a 0–100 grade, the cast is safe after confirming 0 <= value <= 100, even on systems where int is smaller than 32 bits.

sections.title: Report the original line
sections.body: For invalid input, print the required line number and original line content to stderr; trim the line-ending delimiter only if the output format requires it. Return a failure status from main after releasing opened files and allocated buffers.

examples.description: Validates an already-read complete line, preserves its original text for diagnostics, and stores an int only on success. The helper returns 1/0 by its own design; other C functions use different return conventions.

topics.name: * and &: declarations versus pointer expressions
topics.summary: See exactly when * declares a pointer, & obtains an address, and * accesses a value.
topics.description: The same characters can have different roles depending on their position in C code. Compare declarations to expressions and track the type of every result. These examples use ISO C99 pointers to int.

sections.title: In a declaration
sections.body: int x = 5; declares an int. int *p; declares a pointer to int. The * in int *p is declaration syntax; it does not dereference anything. int *a, b; declares only a as a pointer and b as a plain int.

sections.title: At initialization
sections.body: int *p = &x; combines two roles: the declaration * says p is an int*, while the expression &x obtains x's address to store in p. & is not the syntax for declaring a C pointer.

sections.title: After declaration
sections.body: p is the pointer (type int*). *p is x itself through p (type int), so int copy = *p reads x and *p = 9 changes x. &x again produces an int*; &p produces an int** because p is also a variable with an address.

sections.title: In a scanf call
sections.body: scanf("%d", &x) receives an int* and stores the converted number in x. If p already points to x, scanf("%d", p) is also valid. scanf("%d", *p) is wrong because *p is an int, not an int*.

sections.title: Keep other meanings separate
sections.body: In expressions a * b multiplies numbers and a & b performs bitwise AND on integer operands. This guide discusses unary & (address-of) and unary * (dereference), plus * in pointer declarations.

examples.description: Reading *p copies the old value; assigning *p changes x through the pointer.
